title: Sort machined blocks with a two-limit go/no-go gauge
instruction: Check each block, lying flat, with the two-bar gauge: put blocks that slide under the green GO bar but not under the red NO-GO bar in the green ACCEPT tray, blocks that don't fit under the GO bar in the red OVERSIZE tray, and blocks that also slide under the NO-GO bar in the blue UNDERSIZE tray.
context: Unlike a single-limit fit check, this needs both limits of a real two-limit gauge: every block is tried under the GO bar (is it oversize?) and then under the lower NO-GO bar (is it undersize?), and goes to one of three trays; gauging with either bar alone scores 0. Two-limit gauging is routine inspection on a machine-shop floor; the three heights are 3.5 mm apart, too close to judge reliably by eye.
setup: Two arms 61 cm apart on a table; positions are from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward and y to the left, in cm; sizes are length (x) x width (y) x height. Six bare machined aluminium blocks (silver-grey) lie flat on the table, long side along x, in two rows. Front row at x = 10: block 1 (6.4 x 4.4 x 3.20 cm, 0.243 kg) at y = 8, block 2 (6.0 x 4.2 x 3.55, 0.242 kg) at y = 0, block 3 (5.4 x 4.1 x 3.90, 0.233 kg) at y = -8. Back row at x = 17.5: block 4 (5.6 x 4.1 x 3.90, 0.242 kg) at y = 8, block 5 (5.6 x 4.0 x 3.20, 0.194 kg) at y = 0, block 6 (5.5 x 4.0 x 3.55, 0.211 kg) at y = -8. Each block is numbered on its underside. A fixed steel bridge gauge, its near face at x = 31, 2 cm deep: three dark grey steel posts 2 x 2 cm centred at y = 12, 0 and -12; on the left a green-painted steel GO bar (1 cm thick, from y = 1 to 13) with its underside 3.75 cm above the table, on the right a red-painted steel NO-GO bar (1 cm thick, from y = -13 to -1) with its underside 3.40 cm above the table, each over a 10 cm wide lane between posts. Fixed plastic trays with 1 cm walls 3 cm tall and a 0.4 cm floor, inside sizes along x by y, all centred at x = 30: a green ACCEPT tray, inside 16 x 18 cm, at y = 27; on the right one tray split by a 1 cm divider at y = -26.5 into a red OVERSIZE half (inside 16 x 10.5 cm, centred at y = -20.75, inboard) and a blue UNDERSIZE half (inside 16 x 10.5 cm, centred at y = -32.25, outboard).
scoring: Only the final sort is scored; the gauge passes themselves aren't. A block is in a tray (or tray half) when its centre is inside that tray's walls, its underside is within 1.5 cm of the tray floor (so a block stacked on another or lying on a wall doesn't count), it is still (under 1 cm/s), and both fingertip centres are at least 2 cm from it; any orientation counts. Its right tray: ACCEPT for the 3.55 cm blocks (2 and 6: under the GO bar, not under the NO-GO bar), OVERSIZE for the 3.90 cm blocks (3 and 4), UNDERSIZE for the 3.20 cm blocks (1 and 5). A block in any other tray, or off the table, is wrong. Score = (blocks in their right tray - 3 x wrong blocks) / 6, but not below 0, so 0, 1/6, ..., 1; blocks anywhere else on the table count neither way. Leaving everything scores 0, so does putting every block in one tray, gauging with only one bar (two blocks wrong) or swapping OVERSIZE and UNDERSIZE. Over every blind strategy (sending blocks to trays without telling them apart), the best expected score is 0.056 (one block in a tray) and the average 0.011. 1.0 when all six are in their right trays; the trial then ends once that has held for 1 s. On real arms, judge from a top-down photo after the arms withdraw, reading each block's number on its underside.
reset_notes: Put the six blocks back flat at their positions in the two rows (numbers as listed, long side along x).
fidelity: Approximate. The limits are exaggerated: real gauges split hundredths of a millimetre; here the heights are 3.5 mm apart, a passing block clears its bar by 2 mm and a blocked one is 1.5 mm too tall, as tighter fits are unreliable in the simulator. The gauge and trays are fixed. The blocks are rigid uniform boxes; the simulator gives loose objects rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than bare aluminium on steel.
